extracted.intended_audience: interest-group advocates, policy practitioners, and scholars studying notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Drafting comments submitted to federal agency rule dockets intended to influence final rule content by using empirically supported features (specificity, consistency, usable textual proposals, and new information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of commenter preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: When comments cluster around a consistent direction of change, agencies move the rule that way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective comments align with similar arguments from other commenters or explicitly acknowledge and address opposing positions. Building a consistent record across multiple commenters increases the likelihood that agencies will adopt the advocated change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of requested change
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments that requested particular textual changes to the proposed rule were more likely to be reflected in the final rule than diffuse policy objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid generic objections; identify concrete changes rather than broad positions. Specific requests make it easier for agencies to translate comment content into final-rule language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request a specific change to a specific paragraph/section
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment request a specific change to a specific paragraph/section of the proposed rule (rather than a generic position)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to exact regulatory citations, paragraph numbers, or sections. The more precisely the comment locates the text to be changed, the more actionable it is for agency staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide the agency with textual language for adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment provide the agency with the textual language it could adopt for the change being requested?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply draft regulatory text or redlined language that an agency could insert directly into the rule; this lowers the drafting cost for the agency and increases the chance of adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect to or anticipate other commenters to build a consistent record
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment connect to or anticipate other commenters' likely positions to build a consistent record?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference allied submissions, coordinate framing or evidence across multiple comments, or explicitly respond to anticipated counterarguments to create a coherent, reinforcing narrative in the docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate magnitude of harm or benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment estimate the magnitude of harm/benefit from the proposed change vs. the alternative?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide quantitative or reasoned qualitative estimates of costs, harms, benefits, or distributional effects comparing the proposal and alternatives. Clear impact estimates make the request more persuasive and actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply information the agency does not already possess
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment supply information the agency does not already possess (cost data, operational impact, downstream effects)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide original empirical data, operational details, cost estimates, implementation burdens, or downstream consequences. New, concrete information is particularly influential because it fills gaps in the agency's knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat comments as direct mechanisms of policy change (targeting the docket)
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-targeted comment to the docket is not 'shouting into the void' — comments themselves are mechanisms of policy change, not only conduits to Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target the comment to the agency's decision-making needs: address the administrative record, explain statutory or technical implications, and make clear why the agency should adopt the proposed change. Assume agency staff will read and use actionable submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emulate organized-interest structural features when acting individually
rubrics_metrics.description: Yackee's sample over-represents formal organized interests; individual commenters can succeed when they emulate the structural features organized interests use: specificity, consistency, and providing usable agency input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are an individual or small actor, strive to adopt the same practices as larger organized groups: coordinate language, supply draft regulatory text, include concrete evidence, and align your framing with other commenters to increase impact.
